newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr pressed flat by Japanese masses.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr pressed flat by Japanese masses.

text.p: The Australian dollar finished Wednesday plastered to 12-month lows as a mass of Japanese offers overshadowed favourable domestic developments.

The currency had tried to rally when the Reserve Bank all but ruled out a near term rate cut. And the economy won what was effectively a policy easing anyway, when the country's biggest housing lender slashed its mortgage rates to 24 year lows.

But intimations of steady policy and future growth held little appeal with trend-following Japanese investors. They were set on using the opportunity of a weak yen to exit long A$ positions at a profit and re-invest in higher yielding havens.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local dollar had crumpled to US$0.7558/63 its lowest close since February last year, from an early US$0.7581/86 and US$0.7583/88 late here Tuesday.
Traders said the currency had found good bids around the US$0.7555 area so far, partly from exporters and partly from banks protecting knock-out options at US$0.7550.

The latter are only activated if a currency breaks the strike level and requires the option writer to pay out a fixed amount. Dealers said the banks would probably not have covered their exposure when writing the options and would have to sell dollars to meet their obligations should they be triggered.
Such an event, combined with the weight of Tokyo offers, could see the currency test US$0.7500/10 support, they added.

The Japanese urge to sell has been linked to upcoming maturities of yen/A$ samurai bonds launched in the last two years. However, the actual amounts maturing were relatively modest with a single 20 billion yen issue due Thursday, a 50 billion yen bond in March and a pause then until October.

Rather, analysts reckoned the exodus reflected the early redemption of samurais by Japanese retail investors and the subsequent cutting of A$ exposure by the securities houses that launched the bonds.
In contrast, the local dollar was up on most crosses as economic troubles in Germany and Japan made Australia's growth slowdown look positively benign in comparison.

It jumped to 1.2753/65 marks from 1.2595/11 as the dramatic rise in German unemployment reported last week stoked talk the Bundesbank would either have to cut rates again and/or allow a further depreciation in the mark.

The currency also firmed to 94.00/10 yen from 93.33/43, in part aping a rampant U.S. dollar which climbed above 124.00 yen. These gains helped it rise to 58.1 on the trade weighted index from a previous 58.0 close.

The outlook for the domestic economy was also improving, according to RBA governor Ian Macfarlane who saw enough signs of a pickup to say it was logical to wait on developments on the wages front before deciding whether change policy again.

The need for further official action was also lessened by intensifying competition in the once cosy banking sector which saw the Commonwealth Bank slash mortgage rates by 0.7 point today to 7.55 percent without the RBA lifting a finger.
The move was expected to be matched by the other major banks and would put cash directly in the pockets of homeowners, so supporting consumer spending and sentiment, said analysts.

Such support was timely given that the Westpac consumer sentiment index for February out today showed a surprisingly steep 7.9 percent fall. The sting was drawn somewhat by back revisions which showed January rose 6.0 percent indstead of 4.0 percent and December fell 5.3 percent instead of 6.7 percent.
Westpac itself said such swings in sentiment generally preceded major sustained movements in the index and in this case it suspected the eventual trend would be upwards.
Nevertheless, dealers cautioned a weak January jobs number on Thursday would provide ammunition for those still calling for a rate cut. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
